Deposits at every FDIC-insured bank are.why: The $250,000 limit is the best-known fact about US deposit insurance; banks print it on their websites and statements.

sources.quote: FDIC deposit insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category.

Deposits at Dollar Bank are insured up t.why: The bank is named with its products, not with the federal limit. Exact forms of the direct statement are absent or nearly so; the only hit for 'Dollar Bank is insured' is one advertising page (indexed twice) reading 'Each depositor at Dollar Bank is insured to $250,000 by the FDIC', against 14,583 mentions of the bank, so a member-specific form of the limit does exist once. The AND hits for 'Dollar Bank AND FDIC' that were sampled are account advertisements without the limit. A review found that two earlier counts ('Dollar Bank deposits' 0 and 'Dollar Bank AND $250,000' 0) contradicted that page (it holds both strings within a few tokens), so they were removed; re-queried on 2026-11-12, 'Dollar Bank AND $250,000' still returns 0 although the page has both within a few tokens, so AND counts on this bank are unreliable and are not used; the same two counts sit in finance-replace-d005, which is not edited here. Common sense: people say 'deposits at FDIC-insured banks are insured up to $250,000' and that a given bank is FDIC-insured; nobody states the limit for one particular bank on its own, though it is true.

notes: Dev TBox contraction, paired with the revision finance-replace-d005 (README, Contraction: 'The three operations are paired'): it removes that revision's original rule, that deposits at every FDIC-insured bank are insured up to $250,000 per depositor (same class, relation and old value). It replaces the earlier one-dollar-note contraction (bears_portrait_of), kept only as a source of ideas. The direct, paraphrase and cross-lingual questions are the revision's, asked of the original rule; like the revision, each names a single-ownership account, so the per-category rule never gives a second fair answer. Its own questions become 'does not know'; under strong Kleene logic so do the three propositional ones (the FDIC side facts are the revision's). The three derived queries are the revision's, with the same small banks named in the prompt as FDIC members (inheritance, 2 hops, membership in the prompt): before, the rule gives $250,000 (and $350,000 uncovered of $600,000); after, nothing does. The banks were chosen in the revision because their own text does not state the limit (Emigrant Bank was dropped for that reason; Dollar Bank has one advertising page that states the limit, recorded in its evidence, where two contradicting zero counts were removed after review, since AND counts are unreliable for it; the same counts remain in finance-replace-d005, which is not edited here), so no member-specific stored fact keeps the old answer. Residual risk, recorded: the $250,000 figure is famous and repeated per bank in advertising generally, so a model may keep it through the number's fame rather than the rule. Unrelated near asks the NCUA credit-union limit ($250,000 as well): an edit that over-removes deposit-insurance knowledge would lose it; contraction is exempt from Rule 7. Evidence and checks are the revision's (same facts, same counts). The rule has held since 2010, with no exception among members.
